hook: The scholar king who gave Korea its own alphabet.

pages.x: Yi Do was the third son of the king of Joseon Korea. He read so much that when he fell ill his father had his books taken away; he found one left behind a screen and read it over and over. His father passed over his elder brothers and made him king in 1418, at 21.

He gathered Korea's best scholars in the Hall of Worthies to study science, history and government. He had farming manuals rewritten to suit Korea's own climate, and pushed the northern border out to the Yalu and Tumen rivers.
In 1443 he created a new alphabet for Korean, with 28 letters whose shapes show how the mouth makes each sound. Before, Koreans wrote in difficult Chinese characters.
pages.fx: "A wise man can learn them in a morning; even a fool in ten days." Hangul made Korea one of the most literate countries on Earth.

pages.x: With the inventor Jang Yeong-sil, once a slave, he built sundials, water clocks that struck the hours by themselves, and standard rain gauges set up all over the country.
pages.fx: Korea kept careful records of rainfall to plan farming and taxes, among the oldest weather records in the world.

pages.x: Many officials hated the new alphabet. Real scholars, they said, wrote Chinese, and easy writing for common people would only cause trouble. Sejong argued back himself. A later king banned Hangul for a time, but it survived.
He worked so hard that he suffered from diabetes and eye disease, and went almost blind. He died in 1450, aged 53.
Sejong is the most admired ruler in Korean history. His alphabet is used by 80 million people, Hangul Day is a national holiday, and his statue sits in the heart of Seoul.
